How to use this book

This book follows a journey. Some years ago a small party of travellers went round Egypt and Turkey with a teacher of the Buddha’s teaching, Acharn Sujin of Thailand. They saw the pyramids, the tombs of the Egyptian kings, golden treasures in museums, and the waters of the Bosporus at Istanbul. They also lost their luggage, grew tired and hungry, waited for hours at airports, and fell ill before a flight. All the way, in the bus, in a horse coach, on a boat and on the plane, they talked about the Buddha’s teaching, and one of them, Nina van Gorkom, wrote the talks down. Her book is called A Journey with Dhamma in Egypt and Turkey. This book retells it for young readers in twelve chapters.

Pāḷi words. The Buddha’s teaching was written down in a language called Pāḷi. You will meet Pāḷi words all through this book. Every time one appears, its English meaning sits right next to it in brackets, like this: citta (consciousness), paññā (understanding). You never have to remember a Pāḷi word to understand the page. But if you do remember a few, you will be able to read the ancient texts one day.

Saying the words. A line over a letter makes it long: ā sounds like the “a” in “father”, ī like the “ee” in “see”, ū like the “oo” in “moon”. A dot under a letter (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ) means you curl your tongue back a little. ñ sounds like the “ny” in “canyon”. ṃ sounds like “ng”. So paññā is said “pan-nyaa” and satipaṭṭhāna is said “sa-ti-pat-thaa-na”.

Who is speaking. Nina wrote her book in the first person: “we walked”, “I was so impatient”. This book tells the story in the third person, so it says “Nina” and “the travellers”. But whenever words stand in quotation marks, they are the exact words of Nina’s book, or of Acharn Sujin, Gabi, Alan or Ms Tuna as Nina wrote them down, or of the ancient texts she quotes. Nothing in quotation marks has been changed.

Hard words. Some English words in this book are hard. The first time a hard word is met in a chapter it has a small number after it, like this: aeons⁵. Its meaning is given at the end of the chapter, under “Hard words in this chapter”, and all the hard words are listed together at the back, after the word list. In the web edition, tapping or clicking on the word shows its meaning.

Quizzes. After every two chapters there is a short quiz.

Where it comes from. The book this one follows was published by Zolag and may be freely copied, so long as its contents are not changed. Nina made the journey, she says, “some twenty years ago”, long before she wrote the book. The pictures of the journey keep to that time, and the pictures of stories from the ancient texts keep to the Buddha’s time.

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  3

Introduction: the travellers and the road

“Gabi, Alan and I had opportunities for Dhamma discussions with Acharn Sujin while we were walking along the pyramids of Gizeh”

The teacher. Acharn Sujin is a teacher of the Buddha’s teaching who lives in Bangkok, in Thailand. “Acharn” is the Thai word for teacher. People come from all over the world to listen to her, and on this journey she travelled with them to Egypt and Turkey. She does not teach from a book. She asks questions about what is happening right now: “Do you like it to be tired?”

The writer. Nina van Gorkom comes from Holland. She has written many books that explain the Buddha’s teaching in plain words, and she has listened to Acharn Sujin for many years. Her husband is called Lodewijk. He stayed at home, but he comes into the talks more than once, because Acharn uses him to make a point: “You assume that there is Lodewijk, but you just enjoy paññatti, a concept1.”

The friends. Two other friends had joined the tour: “Gabi from Germany and Alan from England”. Gabi reads the Jātakas (the stories of the Buddha’s former births) and finds herself in them. Alan has to travel a long way on his own to hear the teaching; his family and friends are not interested. On the plane the three of them interviewed one another about the Buddha’s teaching, and two chapters of the book are their questions and answers.

The guide. In Turkey the party had a guide, Ms Tuna. She was a Muslim and believed in God and in a soul. On a boat on the Bosporus, Acharn Sujin talked with her about seeing and hearing, about sleeping and dreaming, and about what a soul might be. That talk is Chapter 9.

The places. In Egypt the travellers walked “along the pyramids of Gizeh”, went round “the tombs of the Egyptian kings”, looked at golden treasures in museums, and sat for long hours in the bus and at Cairo airport. In Turkey they visited Istanbul and took a boat on the Bosporus. The talks happened “in papyrus2

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  4

Page 4
Journey A Journey with Dhamma for (p. 1–15) p. 5

shops, in handicraft shops, in restaurants, in the bus, in a horse coach, on a boat or on the plane”. The scenery changed all the time. The subject did not.

on land on water in the air

the pyramids of Gizeh, a boat on the Bosporus the flights between the tombs of the kings, the bus at Istanbul Egypt and Turkey

“Right understanding can be developed no matter where one is, on land, on water or in the air.”

What the book is about. It is not a guidebook. It is about what happened in the minds of the travellers while they looked at the pyramids, waited for their luggage and felt tired. Acharn Sujin’s reminder, which runs through the whole book, is that “everything is just “dhamma”, a reality3 that is conditioned4, in whatever situation one may be”. The chapters take her reminders one by one: patience, the present moment, the wish to be mindful5, what a soul is, and what the Buddha’s teaching says to someone who asks about it for the first time.

Chapter 1: Everything is dhamma

Nina’s book begins with a sentence that could stand over the whole journey: “Right understanding can be developed no matter where one is, on land, on water or in the air.” The travellers were on land when they walked along the pyramids of Gizeh, on water when they took a boat on the Bosporus, and in the air when they flew between Egypt and Turkey. In all three places they talked with Acharn Sujin about the Buddha’s teaching.

“The scenery changed all the time, but we were reminded that everything that appears is a dhamma, a conditioned reality.”

Different sights, the same seeing. Nina writes: “The scenery changed all the time, but we were reminded that everything that appears is a dhamma, a conditioned1 reality2.” A traveller sees a pyramid, then a shop full of papyrus3, then the inside of a bus. These are very different sights. But in each case there is seeing, and seeing is the same kind of reality wherever it happens. “Seeing sees visible object4 now, and also aeons5 ago there was seeing of visible object, and there will be seeing in the future, for aeons to come.” An aeon is a stretch of time too long to count.

Pleasant and unpleasant. “We experienced6 pleasant feeling when we were seeing objects of art and unpleasant feeling when we were tired or when the luggage was lost.” Acharn Sujin’s answer to both was the same. She “explained to us that everything is just “dhamma”, a reality that is conditioned, in whatever situation one may be”. Pleasant feeling is a dhamma (reality). Unpleasant feeling is a dhamma (reality). Neither lasts, and neither belongs to anyone.

The word dhamma. The Pāḷi word dhamma (reality) is the most important word in the book, and it has more than one meaning. Nina explains:

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  6

Page 6
Journey A Journey with Dhamma for (p. 1–15) p. 7

“When we speak about the “Dhamma” we mean the Buddha’s teaching of all that is real. The phenomena7 that occur at this moment and that can be experienced through the senses and the mind can be called “dhammas”, conditioned realities.”

So with a capital letter, the Dhamma (the teaching) is what the Buddha taught. With a small letter, a dhamma (reality) is anything real that can be experienced right now: seeing, hearing, a sound, hardness, a feeling, a thought. It is “conditioned”: it arises8 because of causes and cannot arise without them.

dhamma one word, two meanings

Dhamma, with a capital letter dhammas, with a small letter “the Buddha's teaching of all that is real” “conditioned realities” what the Buddha taught, kept in the Tipiṭaka seeing, hearing, sound, feeling, thinking happening at this moment, arising because of causes

“The word “dhamma” has several meanings.”

Mind and body are not what they seem. Most people think of their mind and their body as two things that last. Nina writes: “We cling9 to ideas of mind and body that exist, but in reality, what we take for the body or the mind are ever changing dhammas that fall away10 immediately and that are not owned by a self.” What is called “my mind” is one moment of experiencing after another. What is called “my body” is hardness, heat, motion and the other qualities of matter11, arising and falling away. There is no owner behind them.

Conditions. The Buddha taught the conditions12 for everything that happens. Nina gives seeing as the example:

“Nobody can cause the arising of seeing, seeing has its own conditions for its arising. Without eyesense and visible object it could not arise.”

Eyesense is the fine matter in the eye that can receive colour. Visible object is colour, that which can be seen. When the two meet, seeing arises. Nobody decides to see. In the same way, liking or disliking what is seen is conditioned too: “they arise because of attachment13 and aversion14 that arose in the past”. A person who has been attached to pretty things a thousand times before will be attached again when a golden necklace appears in a museum case.

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  7

Page 7
Journey A Journey with Dhamma for (p. 1–15) p. 8

eyesense the fine matter in the eye nobody decides to see seeing “Nobody can cause the arising of seeing, seeing has a citta (consciousness) its own conditions for its arising.” arises when both meet visible object colour, that which can be seen

“Without eyesense and visible object it could not arise.”

Not theory. Nina and her friends had read many books about the Buddha’s teaching and listened to tapes of talks. But reading was not enough: “we also need to be reminded of realities in the different situations of our daily life. Then we can see more clearly that everything we learn is not mere theory, that it is all about daily realities.” That is why a journey makes a good school. The luggage is lost, the bus is late, the shower in the hotel does not work. Each of these is a moment to find out what the mind is doing.

The three baskets. The Buddha’s teachings are kept in the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets). Nina names the three: “the Vinaya or Book of Discipline for the monks15, the Suttanta or Discourses16 and the Abhidhamma which is an exposition of all realities in detail.” The Abhidhamma (the higher teaching) takes everything apart and names each piece: each kind of consciousness17, each mental factor18, each kind of matter. It can sound like a book for scholars19. Nina says it is not: “The Abhidhamma deals with whatever is experienced in daily life; it deals with what is pleasant or unpleasant, wholesome20 or unwholesome21.” And she gives Acharn Sujin’s own saying: ““The Abhidhamma is not in the book”, as Acharn said.” The

book describes seeing; seeing itself is happening now.

What the next chapter does. Before the story goes on, a few of the Pāḷi words that Acharn Sujin used need explaining: citta (consciousness), cetasika (mental22 factor), nāma (mind), rūpa (matter), kusala (wholesome), akusala (unwholesome) and vipāka (result23). Chapter 2 explains them in Nina’s own words.

Chapter 2: What a person really is

In Turkey the travellers’ guide believed that each person has a soul that lasts. Nina writes: “Very gently Acharn explained to her that what she called soul was in fact a mental1 state or citta that changes all the time and that arises2 because of conditions3. This is the teaching of the Abhidhamma.” Here are the words Acharn Sujin used, one at a time.

Citta. A citta (consciousness4) is a moment of experiencing5 something. Seeing is a citta (consciousness); so is hearing; so is thinking. “Citta is a reality6 and it arises throughout our life. Only one citta arises at a time and it is accompanied by several mental factors7, cetasikas.” One at a time: there is never seeing and hearing in the same moment, however quickly they follow one another.

Cetasika. Each citta (consciousness) is accompanied by cetasikas (mental factors) that arise and fall away8 with it. “Cetasikas such as feeling or remembrance9 accompany each type of citta.” Feeling is a cetasika (mental factor): every moment of consciousness has some feeling, pleasant, unpleasant or neither. Saññā (remembrance) is another: it marks what is experienced so that it can be recognised again.

cetasikas (mental factors) arise and fall away together with each citta feeling

concentration saññā (remembrance) citta consciousness one at a time attention contact

intention some are kusala (wholesome): kindness, understanding some are akusala (unwholesome): ignorance, attachment, aversion “Only one citta arises at a time and it is accompanied by several mental factors, cetasikas.”

Wholesome, unwholesome, and neither.

“Citta and its accompanying cetasikas can be good or wholesome10, kusala, they can be evil or unwholesome11, akusala, or they can be neither kusala nor akusala. Akusala cetasikas such as ignorance12, attachment13 and aversion14 accompany akusala citta. Wholesome cetasikas such as kindness or understanding accompany kusala citta.”

So kusala (wholesome) means good: a moment of kindness, of generosity15, of understanding. Akusala (unwholesome) means bad: a moment of lobha (attachment), of dosa (aversion), of moha (ignorance). These three are the roots of all that is unwholesome. A moment of seeing or hearing is neither kusala (wholesome) nor akusala (unwholesome); it is simply the experience of what is there.

Nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter). Everything real is one of two kinds. “Citta and cetasika are mental phenomena16, nāma. Mental phenomena experience an object17. Physical phenomena or rūpa do not experience any object.” Nāma (mind) experiences: seeing experiences colour, hearing experiences sound.

A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers  ·  10

Page 10
Journey A Journey with Dhamma for (p. 1–15) p. 11

Rūpa (matter18) experiences nothing: colour does not know that it is seen, the hardness of a chair knows nothing at all. The test is simple. Does it experience something? Then it is nāma (mind). Does it experience nothing? Then it is rūpa (matter).

Two kinds of truth. This is the hardest idea in the chapter and the one Acharn Sujin returned to most often.

“We should know the difference between ultimate19 truth and conventional20 truth. Conventional truth is the world of concepts21 such as person, tree or animal we can think of but which are not real in the ultimate sense. Ultimate realities, nāma and rūpa, are impermanent22, they arise and fall away.”

A tree is a concept, paññatti (concept): a name for colours that are seen, hardness that is touched, and a memory that puts them together. The word “tree” is useful. But the tree is not what is directly experienced; colour and hardness are. The same goes for “person”. Nina writes: “If the difference between concepts and ultimate realities is not known, the eightfold Path cannot be developed.” The eightfold Path is the Buddha’s way to the end of suffering23, and its purpose is “seeing ultimate realities as impermanent, suffering and non-self24“.

conventional truth ultimate truth the world of concepts, paññatti nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter) person tree animal seeing colour hearing Lodewijk a car Cairo sound feeling hardness thought of, not directly experienced “impermanent, they arise and fall away”

“Conventional truth is the world of concepts such as person, tree or animal we can think of but which are not real in the ultimate sense.”

One object at a time. Right understanding “is developed through direct awareness25 of nāma and rūpa”. When there is awareness of one reality as it appears, through the eyes or the ears or the mind, there is no thought of a whole person or thing at that moment: “we do not think of a concept of a “whole”, of a person or thing, at that moment.”

Kamma (deed) and vipāka (result). Why does one traveller hear harsh words and another kind ones? “Whatever we experience through the senses, be it pleasant or unpleasant, is conditioned26 by kamma, wholesome or unwholesome action committed in the past. Cittas conditioned by kamma are vipākacittas, cittas which are results27.” So a kamma (deed28) done in the past brings a vipāka (result) now: seeing or hearing something pleasant or unpleasant. A vipākacitta (result consciousness) is neither wholesome nor unwholesome in itself. The travellers found this a great help when things went wrong:

“When others behave towards us in a disagreeable way or speak harshly, we may react to this with akusala cittas rooted in aversion. However, when we remember that unpleasant experiences through the senses are vipākacittas conditioned by our own kamma, not by another person, we shall be less

Journey A Journey with Dhamma for (p. 1–15) p. 12

inclined29 to blame others.”

neither of these is a result they are causes, kamma (deeds) “Be patient, receive all kinds of vipākacittas”

kusala citta akusala citta vipākacitta wholesome consciousness unwholesome consciousness result consciousness kindness attachment seeing generosity aversion hearing patience ignorance smelling, tasting understanding impatience touching

kamma (deeds) done in the past “Cittas conditioned by kamma are vipākacittas, cittas which are results.”

Thinking of oneself. Acharn Sujin “would emphasize that we should not think of ourselves, and that we become less selfish by paying more attention to the needs of others.” Nina writes: “This is a simple advice, but it is very basic.” She noticed how often the thought of “I” came in, even into good things: “When kusala citta arises, there is no clinging30, but very shortly after kusala citta has fallen away we are likely to cling to an idea of “my kusala”.” A moment of kindness is kusala (wholesome). The thought of “my kusala” that follows it is not.

Three steps. How does anyone come to understand all this?

“Because of listening to the Dhamma, we acquire intellectual31 understanding of what the Buddha taught and then we gradually learn to verify32 in our life the truth of the phenomena that occur so that there can be direct understanding.”

First, listening. Second, understanding what was heard, which is called intellectual understanding. Third, direct understanding, when the reality itself is known as it appears, not just thought about.

1. listening 2. intellectual understanding 3. direct understanding to the Dhamma of what the Buddha taught of the realities that appear hearing the teaching, understanding what was knowing seeing, hearing, reading, discussing heard and read feeling as they are now

“we gradually learn to verify in our life the truth of the phenomena that occur”

From the very beginning. The Path “should be developed with detachment33 from the idea of self at the very beginning.” A person who sets out to become “somebody with sati” has taken a wrong turning at the first step.
